issues.justification: In context this is a kindergarten teacher on public transport; «проездной» means a transit pass/travel card. 'Pass!' is ambiguous and loses the everyday Soviet setting.

issues.source_quote: Это тебе не мелочь по карманам тырить!
issues.translation_quote: This isn't like nicking loose change from pockets!
issues.justification: The line is a punchy colloquial taunt. 'Nicking loose change from pockets' is clunky and overexplains «тырить», weakening the criminal slang and comic force.
«Тошниловка» is slang for a cheap, grim eatery/dive, not specifically a 'beer hall' and not literally a place for vomiting. The pair is a jargon glossary; the chosen English distorts the meaning.
This is left essentially untranslated/transliterated, so the joke and the character's muddled recollection do not cross into English at all.

«Параша» is prison slang for the cell latrine bucket. 'Toilet bucket' is descriptively understandable, but the loss of the marked prison argot weakens characterization and prison-register specificity.

The translation vacillates between slang registers; 'peepers' is jokey in a way that can work, but throughout the film this recurring threat is iconic criminal argot. The inconsistent rendering weakens its catchphrase quality.
Here «обзовись» means 'give the proper oath / say the formula proving you're one of us.' 'Swear it!' is too vague and misses the underworld test of identity.

The fake escape is for the convicts, not 'for them' in the abstract. The English is understandable but blurs the operational meaning; 'arrange a fake breakout for them' would better preserve the plot detail.

issues.source_quote: если вор не нырнет - голова с плеч!
issues.translation_quote: so if the thief doesn't duck— off comes his head!
issues.justification: The anecdote's joke depends on 'dive' because the thief is immersed in a vat. 'Duck' weakens the visual and undermines the payoff in the next line about spending the day diving into filth.
The source says the driver is an informant/operative planted by police. 'My man' can suggest a subordinate or friend; for plot clarity in a crime-comedy setup, 'one of ours' or 'our man' is needed.
«Проходная» is the factory gate/guardhouse. 'Checkpoint' is too generic and loses the industrial-Soviet setting.

The number is wrong in relation to the source line's function? No—the issue is that without context it is opaque. However elsewhere the translation tends to explicate. Here leaving it unexplained is inconsistent and may confuse viewers; at minimum a more natural line would preserve that he's talking about an additional charge for escape. This is a weaker issue but still impacts comprehension.
English normally does not say 'some trousers' in this context; more importantly he needs a pair of pants/trousers. The phrasing is awkward enough to risk distraction during a comic beat.
Stilted phrasing. In context these are kindergarten heads; 'All principals?' or 'All of you in charge?' would sound more natural in spoken English.

issues.source_quote: против бритвы - пиджак и брюки. Только пиджак.
issues.translation_quote: Jacket and trousers for the razor. Just the jacket.
issues.justification: This is bargaining language in a prison barter scene. The translation is too literal and awkward to the point of obscuring who is offering what in exchange for what.

issues.source_quote: Я сказал клички отставить! Это фамилия, а имя - Василий Алибабаевич
issues.translation_quote: I said no nicknames! That's my last name. My first name is Vasily Alibabayevich
issues.justification: The joke is that 'Ali-Baba' sounds like a criminal nickname but is in fact his surname, while 'Vasily Alibabayevich' is his comic full name/patronymic. Calling it simply 'my first name' is inaccurate and loses the Russian naming humor.
These are work norms/brigade jargon in the radiator-carrying scene. Rendered bare like this, the exchange becomes meaningless in English, losing the comic abruptness and situational sense.
This is a cultural allusion to a well-known film title. Left untranslated without adaptation or signaling, it will not land for most English viewers and the joke fails.

The bureaucratic Soviet phrasing is flattened awkwardly. 'Per diem' is possible, but the pair sounds like modern business English, not period police paperwork; this weakens both meaning and era flavor.

issues.source_quote: Грабителей мы поймали... Шлема не оказалось
issues.translation_quote: We've caught the robbers... The helmet wasn't there
issues.justification: Throughout the film the object is a famous archaeological artifact. Rendering references sometimes as 'helmet', elsewhere as 'hat' ('Если б мы еще шапка принесли!' / 'If only we'd brought the hat too!') is inconsistent and damages continuity.

issues.source_quote: Ты туда не ходи, ты сюда ходи, а то снег башка попадет - совсем мертвый будешь!
issues.translation_quote: Don't go that way, go this way, or snow will hit your head— you'll be dead for good!
issues.justification: This iconic line is intentionally broken Russian from a Central Asian character. The translation makes it grammatical and generic, losing both the character voice and the absurd humor. This is a major style/voice failure.

issues.translation_quote: Politeness is a thief's best weapon
issues.justification: The literal wording is understandable, but the aphoristic comic snap is dulled. In English this lands woodenly rather than as a wry quasi-proverb.
In response to 'Did she die?', «Я умер» is a dry comic line meaning something like 'I might as well have' / 'I died inside.' Literal 'I died' sounds nonsensical rather than bitterly comic.

Not wrong by itself, but elsewhere «засекли», «застукают», «заметут» are all flattened into similar English verbs. The rich variation in criminal colloquial speech is lost, harming voice differentiation.
Barmaley is a specific children's-villain reference. Left unexplained, the humor and tone are lost for non-Russian viewers.
The acronym is merely transliterated. In subtitles, this gives no clue that this is the anti-theft/economic crimes police, impairing comprehension of the joke and situation.

issues.source_quote: Только она думает, что папаша ее ученый и про нас он ей тоже насвистел
issues.translation_quote: Only she thinks her old man is a scientist, and he also fed her a line that we're scientists too.
issues.justification: Reasonably conveys meaning, but it drops the comic bluntness of «папаша» and «насвистел». The criminal, mocking register softens noticeably.

issues.source_quote: Джентльмен удачи! Украл, выпил - в тюрьму. Украл, выпил - в тюрьму. Романтика!
issues.translation_quote: A gentleman of fortune! Stole, drank—back to prison. Stole, drank—back to prison. Romance!
issues.justification: The title phrase is central and idiomatic in Russian cultural context. 'Gentleman of fortune' is literal but wooden; the comic self-mythologizing of the speech is diminished.

issues.source_quote: Шакал я паршивый - у детей деньги отнял, детский сад ограбил!
issues.translation_quote: I'm a lousy jackal—I took money from kids, robbed a kindergarten!
issues.justification: The meaning is there, but 'robbed a kindergarten' in English can imply direct violence against a nursery school. The source is about robbing the institution's funds; the nuance matters for the character's moral panic.

He is criticizing handling of equipment/implements in the house. Singular 'the tool' is unnatural and misleading in English; it sounds like a specific object rather than household/scientific equipment.

issues.translation_quote: We're going to rob an embassy!
issues.justification: Literal but the comic absurdity could be better carried. As rendered, it sounds merely plot-like. The line should land as ridiculous deadpan intimidation.

issues.source_quote: Не выпускать улыбку из открытых глаз
issues.translation_quote: Don't let a smile leave your open eyes
issues.justification: This song line is mistranslated. The source means roughly 'let your open eyes keep smiling' / 'keep the smile in your open eyes.' The English is unidiomatic and semantically off.

In context this is a deliberately blunt, socially humiliating reveal. While semantically correct, the translation misses the social sting; elsewhere 'crook' is used. Inconsistent rendering weakens the scene's impact.

issues.source_quote: Хозяева в Москве. Знаю. Я и есть хозяйка.
issues.translation_quote: The owners are in Moscow. I know. I'm the owner.
issues.justification: The gendered comic reveal of «хозяйка» is flattened by switching from plural 'owners' to singular 'owner.' It sounds clumsy and less playful in English.

issues.translation_quote: Lunch with us on the first
issues.justification: Idiomatic English would be 'Come to lunch on the first.' The current phrasing sounds like a fragment and weakens a warm, socially important invitation.

issues.translation_quote: I will find you for sure.
issues.justification: This recurring menace is iconic and should sound chillingly simple. 'for sure' is too colloquial and weakens the threat.

issues.source_quote: Это тебе, Вася... Гаврила Петрович, это тебе.
issues.translation_quote: These are for you, Vasya... Gavrila Petrovich, these are for you.
issues.justification: The switch from nickname/familiar form to the formalized prison-assigned name is part of the scene's emotional texture. The English misses the self-conscious correction's subtle humor and tenderness.

issues.translation_quote: Vorkuta. Why? I did time there.
issues.justification: This preserves meaning, but the next line «Джамбул... там тепло, там мой дом, там моя мама» relies on parallel emotional contrast. The translation overall underplays the poignancy of this children's-game scene.

issues.translation_quote: Shmire hanged himself. - Came on my own.
issues.justification: «Сам пришел» means 'I came by myself' and is Docent's laconic entrance line, but the English is telegraphic to the point of oddness. It jars instead of sounding menacingly casual.

issues.source_quote: Какая зараза хмыренку этому на Хмыря накапала?
issues.translation_quote: What bastard ratted on this little punk about Shmire?
issues.justification: The line is about someone informing on Khmyr to his child/family. The English 'about Shmire' is vague and does not capture that someone told the boy the truth about his father.

Misspelled pseudo-Italian in Russian is part of colloquial comic flavor. The standardized Italianized form in English loses some of the rough comic texture; also the phrase may feel high-register rather than semi-literate.
Understandable, but 'little hat' sounds odd and childish in English. 'Quite a heavy cap/helmet' would be more natural.

issues.translation_quote: When it gets dark, we move in!
issues.justification: Serviceable, but 'move in' is generic. In a criminal-sting context, 'we take them' or 'we go in' would preserve the sharper action.
Adequate colloquialism, but 'mug' may sound too jaunty; the source is more simply coarse.
Not wrong, but throughout the kindergarten scenes the translation often sounds slightly bookish rather than like lively spoken English for children.

issues.translation_quote: Come on... Come on... don't make trouble...
issues.justification: Natural enough, but the rhythm of nervous appeasement could be better captured with something like 'Easy... easy... don't start.'
This is a recognizable Soviet catchphrase, but the literal translation sounds stiff in English. A more idiomatic rendering could preserve the comic period flavor without sounding unnatural.
A bit too strong; 'toss them on the floor' would better fit the casual spoken register.
Semantically acceptable, but 'that's peanuts' feels slightly modern/Americanized against the Soviet legal discussion.

issues.translation_quote: The New Year's tree is coming up.
issues.justification: Accurate enough, but awkwardly literal. A more natural equivalent would be 'I've got the New Year's party coming up' or similar.

issues.source_quote: Не было у нас такого уговора!
issues.justification: Understandable, though a more idiomatic spoken line here would be 'We never agreed to that!'
Fine in isolation, but the translation alternates among 'crooks', 'thieves', 'robbers', 'bandits' in ways that blur recurring diction and characterization.
The idiom is colorful and physical here; 'full house' is understandable but somewhat detached from the image of the tanker filling up.
Good functional translation, though it smooths over the earthy colloquial force of the original.

issues.source_quote: Автомашину куплю с магнитофоном, пошью костюм с отливом и в Ялту!
issues.translation_quote: I'll buy a car with a tape deck, get a flashy suit made, and off to Yalta!
issues.justification: Mostly good, but 'tape deck' feels anachronistically specific; a vaguer 'tape player' might fit period flavor better.
